name: Kansas

notes: Groceries: the state tax on food for home ended January 1, 2025 (candy, soft drinks, bottled water and supplements count as food); city and county taxes still apply at their full rate.

Liquor stores charge the 8% liquor enforcement tax instead of sales tax, counted here; beer sold by grocery and convenience stores (cereal malt beverage retailers) pays the sales tax instead, which isn't separated (no official figure gives its share).

Drinks served by clubs, caterers, drinking establishments and other liquor licensees pay the 10% liquor drink tax instead of state and local sales tax, on spirits, wine and beer alike (K.S.A. 79-41a02), counted here. Restaurants holding only a cereal malt beverage license sell beer of up to 6% alcohol with the ordinary sales tax and no drink tax; no official figure gives their share of drinks served, so they aren't separated.

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the full rate, on top of excise taxes left out here: $1.29 a pack of cigarettes, 10% of the wholesale price on other tobacco and 5 cents a milliliter of e-liquid.
Barber and beauty services: hair styling and barber services aren't taxed.
Laundry and dry cleaning are taxed (plus a dry cleaning environmental surcharge, left out here); coin-operated laundry isn't.
Motor fuel is exempt from the sales tax and pays a per-gallon tax instead (24 cents for gasoline, 26 cents for diesel, unchanged since 2003), left out here.
Diapers and menstrual products are taxed (2025 and 2026 bills to exempt them died). Kansas has no sales tax holiday.
Hotel stays pay the sales tax plus local transient guest taxes (Kansas City 10%, Overland Park 9%, Wichita 6%), which are not counted here.
The services below are from the Department of Revenue's Pub. KS-1510.
gaps: Special districts add tax in small areas and aren't included: the Department of Revenue's list (Pub. KS-1700, October 1, 2026) has about 233 community improvement districts (0.1% to 3%) and 35 transportation development districts; its 23 STAR bond districts add no rate of their own. Three cover 5% or more of a city's addresses: Medicine Lodge's Streetscape CID (1%, about 13%), Anthony's downtown CID (2%, about 7%) and Cunningham's (2%, about 9%).

Changes from 2027 aren't in the rates: Manhattan's 0.2% street tax ends December 31, 2026 and Johnson County's 0.25% public safety tax in March 2027; the November 3, 2026 votes (Kansas City, Wyandotte County, Manhattan, Lawrence, Valley Center, Emporia and Finney County) could start taxes from April 1, 2027. Each is noted on its page.

2021275: Emporia's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on a 0.25% sales tax for a recreation facility from April 1, 2027 (City of Emporia); it isn't counted here.
2036000: Kansas City's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on a 0.375% sales tax for parks and infrastructure from April 1, 2027 (Unified Government of Wyandotte County and Kansas City, Kansas); it isn't counted here.
2038900: Lawrence's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on raising its transit sales tax from 0.2% to 0.3% from April 1, 2027 (Douglas County election notice); the current rate is used here.
2044250: Manhattan's 0.2% street maintenance sales tax ends December 31, 2026 (City of Manhattan), and its voters decide on November 3, 2026 on a 0.5% tax for streets from April 1, 2027; the current rate is used here.
2073250: Valley Center's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on a 1% public safety sales tax from April 1, 2027 (City of Valley Center); it isn't counted here.
20055: Finney County's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on renewing its 0.25% sales tax for roads (Finney County); the current rate is used here.
20091: Johnson County's 0.25% public safety sales tax expires in March 2027; a court blocked the vote to renew it (as reported by High Plains Public Radio; the county election office lists no renewal question for November 3, 2026), so the county's rate would fall from 1.475% to 1.225% from April 2027 (Johnson County). The current rate is used here.
20209: Wyandotte County's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on a 0.25% sales tax for health care and homelessness (Unified Government); it isn't counted here.

Community improvement, tax increment and STAR bond districts are mapped for Wichita, Topeka and Liberal; Kansas City, Overland Park, Olathe, Lenexa and Lawrence publish no district maps, though the Department of Revenue lists their sales tax districts (Pub. KS-1700). warn.text: Abilene draws many visitors (the Eisenhower Presidential Library), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (1.6%) and its 7 lodging places (0.9 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
Chautauqua County's flag as a visitor economy comes only from homes the Census counts as seasonal (201 of 1,975, 10.2%), which may be hunting places rather than tourism, so read that flag with care.
Anthony's flag as a visitor economy comes only from homes the Census counts as seasonal (170 of 1,298, 13.1%), which may be hunting places rather than tourism, so read that flag with care.
Elk County's flag as a visitor economy comes only from homes the Census counts as seasonal (161 of 1,491, 10.8%), which may be hunting or lake places rather than tourism, so read that flag with care.

Logan County's flag as a visitor economy rests on its 7 lodging places (2.6 per 1,000 residents), mostly motels in Oakley along Interstate 70 that serve travelers as well as visitors to Monument Rocks and Little Jerusalem, so read that flag with care.
Colby may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels along Interstate 70 (13 lodging places, 2.3 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.
Pratt County may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of Pratt's highway motels (20 lodging places, 2.2 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.

Council Grove draws many visitors (the Santa Fe Trail sites and the nearby lake), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: it has no seasonal homes, and its 5 lodging places (2.0 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's lodging cutoff. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Dodge City draws many visitors (Boot Hill and its Old West history, and the Boot Hill Casino), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (0.1%) and its 29 lodging places (1.0 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though one of its 7 census tracts is flagged on its own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Trego County may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels in WaKeeney along Interstate 70 (7 lodging places, 2.5 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.

Kansas City draws many visitors (the Village West stores, the Kansas Speedway and the Hollywood Casino), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (0.4%) and its 45 lodging places (0.3 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though the Village West tract is flagged on its own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Lindsborg draws many visitors (its Swedish heritage and the Messiah Festival), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (2.0%) and its 6 lodging places (1.5 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Phillipsburg may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels on US 36 and US 183 (6 lodging places, 2.6 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.
Pratt may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels on US 54 and US 281 (19 lodging places, 2.6 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.

Wichita draws many visitors (its downtown and Old Town, the river and Exploration Place), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (0.4%) and its 185 lodging places (0.5 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 8 of its 108 census tracts, downtown's among them, are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

programs: Wichita's STAR bond districts (River District Stadium, River Walk, K-96 and Greenwich) aren't mapped, nor are its newest community improvement districts (Orpheum Theatre, from July 1, 2026; SoCe Corner, from April 1, 2026); the Lincoln and Broadway district is mapped but not yet collecting (Department of Revenue, October 2026).
